newsitem.title: USA: To aggressive drivers - leave egos home for holidays.
newsitem.headline: To aggressive drivers - leave egos home for holidays.

text.p: As America prepares for its biggest highway travel day, aggressive drivers -- high-speed lane-changers, tailgaters, horn-honkers, traffic duellists -- are being warned to leave egos at home over Thanksgiving.
Aggressive driving has replaced drunken driving as the most-feared highway threat in the Washington metropolitan area, and is a rising concern nationwide.
Nationally, deaths and injuries attributed to aggressive driving have climbed 51 percent since 1990, according to the American Automobile Association Foundation for Traffic Safety.

"Aggressive driving is taking its toll on American highways and beneath the mangled wreckage, the twisted steel and shattered glass of motor vehicle crashes, is the constant knowledge that most of it could have been easily prevented," Dr. Ricardo Martinez, head of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, said in a statement.
Thursday's Thanksgiving holiday is again expected to be the heaviest travel day of the year with 26.4 million people predicted to be on the road, the most since the AAA started keeping track in 1985.
The heavy traffic often has a grim consequence: 527 people died in highway accidents over the 1995 Thanksgiving weekend.
Not all are caused by aggressive driving, but Stephanie Faul of the AAA Foundation sees the phenomenon, especially in the Washington, D.C., area, as a disturbing reflection on the national psyche.

"There is an overall climate of self-importance (in the Washington area)," Faul said in an a telephone interview. "They come here because of power, and the car is power. When the power is taken away, you feel frustrated."
Lon Anderson, a spokesman for the AAA's Potomac Chapter covering Washington and nearby counties, believes his region is the worst in the United States for aggressive driving.

The Washington area has the country's second-worst road congestion -- New York City is the worst -- and the second-longest average commute, Anderson said. Those two factors combined with the self-importance element can make for monstrous behaviour behind the wheel, he said.
Two cases have been front page news in the last week.

In one, a driver was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for his part in a high-speed automobile duel with another angry commuter that led to a crash on a riverside parkway. Three people, including the other driver, were killed.
In the other, a 3-year-old girl was critically injured in a crash when her father raced another rush-hour driver.

Clifford Winston, who studies driving regulations and other traffic matters at the Brookings Institution, said the fact that vehicles are getting safer may actually fuel the aggressive driving trend. Drivers seek a certain level of risk, Winston said, and feel they can push their own behaviour if their car has features like airbags and seatbelts.

At the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, which aims to curb risky behaviour that costs insurers millions, Allan Williams said the focus should be on technology that can limit two specific kinds of aggressive behaviour.

Williams favours automatic cameras to nab those who run red lights and those who exceed highway speed limits. He said such cameras are already being tried outside the United States but have generally been tangled in bureaucratic red tape here.
Williams acknowledges these would do little to stop drivers who change lanes at high speed, overtake others with inadequate warning or space or engage in confrontations.
For those who encounter such drivers, NHTSA's Martinez has advice: put your pride aside, do not react in kind or return gestures, avoid eye contact. And get the license number.
